yarn-dinkum.meaning: Every instruction survives in order: straining through muslin, three gallons, the overflow sign, the vent hole, the two pet cocks, the lever notches. The metric glosses "(near enough 11 litres)" and "(about 38-litre)" hang off the original's figures. "brand-spankin'-new car" is colour on 'new car'.
yarn-dinkum.sense: "under its own steam" for under its own power, "topped up" for replenished, "bunged up" for plugged up, "more grunt it puts out" for greater power, "well and truly limbered up" for thoroughly limbered up: all fit. "medium light, top-quality petrol engine oil" correctly localises gas engine oil.
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Natural Aussie: "have a crack at startin' the car", "dead volatile and gets around quick smart", "make bloody sure", "filled up proper". Spellings are Australian ("vapour", "carburettor", "spilt").
yarn-dinkum.register: A strong Aussie voice throughout with dropped g's and slang, swearing mild ("make bloody sure"), within vulgarity 2. Still reads as an instruction text rather than a full pub yarn: "All the other parts of the car are oiled proper when it leaves the factory."
yarn-dinkum.tone: Stays a practical, careful set of instructions: "but whatever you do, don't ever let it get below the lower cock", "Be careful not to advance the spark lever too far".
yarn-dinkum.flow: Reads smoothly: "Keep pourin' the water in till you're sure both the radiator and the cylinder water jackets are full."
yarn-dinkum.variety: Varied ("have a crack", "muck", "topped up", "quick smart", "bunged up", "grunt"), with "cos" used four times as the connective ("cos the vapour", "cos the air", "cos that'd stop", "cos the engine may").
yarn-dinkum.essence: Unmistakably the 1919 manual's question-and-answer drill, headings and cross-references kept: "(See Cut No. 18, also chapter on Lubrication.)"

yarn-troppo.meaning: All instructions survive. Additions are mostly colour: "Now listen, cos this bit's serious", "which is her tellin' ya you've gone too far". "if you can get it clean outta the tank" assumes a rainwater tank the original doesn't mention, and the opener "You'll like this one." hangs off nothing.
yarn-troppo.sense: "chockers" for full, "top-shelf petrol engine oil" for high-grade, "a good slug" for a supply, "you'll get the best outta her" for best results: all fit.
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Very natural: "Keep pourin' till you're dead certain both the radiator and the cylinder water jackets are chockers", "the faster she runs and the more grunt she gives ya". "You'll like this one." reads as a stock opener.
yarn-troppo.register: Full yarn weight: the car is 'her', asides address the listener ("Now listen, cos this bit's serious"), slang throughout; swearing mild ("make bloody sure"), within vulgarity 2.
yarn-troppo.tone: Keeps the practical, safety-minded tone, and flags the serious bit explicitly: "Now listen, cos this bit's serious". "You'll like this one." is an odd jaunty start for a pre-start checklist.
yarn-troppo.flow: Reads well aloud: "Pour the oil in nice and slow till it runs out the upper cock." A few lines run long: "the further you pull this lever down toward yourself in the driver's seat".
yarn-troppo.variety: Well varied: "whip the cap off", "lay your hands on", "chockers", "top-shelf", "good slug", "bunged up", "grunt", "Give it a few goes".
yarn-troppo.essence: Clearly the manual's drill, retold by someone talking you through it: "Get down under the car to the flywheel casin'".

dinkum-3.meaning: All instructions kept. "Once the engine's been well and truly run in" renders 'thoroughly limbered up' in its sense for a new engine. "(the tank that holds this oil)" for the reservoir is fine. "sets off the petrol mix" for 'explodes the gas' is accurate.
dinkum-3.sense: "get yer mitts on" for obtain, "bungs up" for obstructing, "run in" for limbered up, "the more grunt ya get" for greater power: all fit. "it's a beaut idea" for 'a good plan' fits but strains slightly in a technical line.
dinkum-3.authenticity: Natural throughout: "First things first", "watch yerself strikin' a match anywhere near spilt petrol", "start her properly". Australian spellings ("carburettor", "litres").
dinkum-3.register: A solid Aussie voice with dropped g's and slang, but no swearing at all where vulgarity 2 is allowed, and the safety lines stay plain ("make sure there's no naked flames"). Somewhat under full pub-yarn weight.
dinkum-3.tone: Practical and careful: "Just take care not to advance the spark lever too far".
dinkum-3.flow: Reads cleanly, including the merged lever lines: "Usually ya want the spark lever in about the third or fourth notch of the quadrant (the notched half-circle the levers work on), and the throttle opened about five or six notches."
dinkum-3.variety: Varied: "get yer mitts on", "muck", "bungs up", "beaut idea", "hands down", "run in", "grunt".
dinkum-3.essence: Recognisably the manual, headings kept, told as a mate's walk-through: "Get down under the car and in the flywheel casing".

engine.meaning: The original's content survives almost word for word. "After the engine has become flamin' limbered up" changes 'thoroughly' into an intensifier with a different sense.
engine.sense: "flamin' limbered up" puts flamin' where 'thoroughly' meant completely; "the vapour is flamin' volatile'n travels rapidly" uses flamin' as a pun on fire that grates. "bunged up" fits.
engine.authenticity: Mostly the 1919 English with dropped g's and a few insertions ("brand-spankin'-new car", "outta the overflow pipe"), and US forms left in: "What about Gasoline?", "to the carburetor", "high-grade gas engine oil".
engine.register: Largely untranslated: "Upon receipt of the car see that a supply of medium light, high-grade gas engine oil is poured", "the best results will be obtained by carrying the oil". Far under a level-5 brief.
engine.tone: The original's formal instructional tone stays ("Care should be taken not to advance the spark lever too far"), with the odd insertion jarring against it.
engine.flow: Formal sentences broken by insertions: "the vapour is flamin' volatile'n travels rapidly", "(petrol'n air)", "it's advisable to strain it".
engine.variety: Little slang, leaning on flamin' twice and dropped g's: "flamin' volatile'n", "flamin' limbered up".
engine.essence: It is the original nearly verbatim, so its shape survives: "What must be done before startin' the Car?"

unharnessed.meaning: All instructions survive. "and you'll blow your arse to kingdom come" elaborates the explosive vapour warning; "and give you a hell of a whack" elaborates back kick. Both hang off the original. "Don't run the car under its own steam unless the water system's been filled, full stop." keeps the emphasis.
unharnessed.sense: "under its own steam", "dead sure", "get around fast", "the more grunt you get", "loosened up" for limbered up: all fit. "top-quality gas engine oil" leaves the US gas where petrol is meant.
unharnessed.authenticity: Natural, plain Australian talk: "make bloody sure", "beats hard water hands down", "spilt petrol", "carburettor". "gas engine oil" is the one US form left.
unharnessed.register: Casual, clearly Australian, with vulgarity-2 swearing ("blow your arse to kingdom come"), but the slang is light for level 5: "Leave the cock open till it stops running, then shut it."
unharnessed.tone: The practical tone holds; the safety warnings get punchier but stay warnings: "don't you dare, under any circumstances, let it drop below the bottom cock".
unharnessed.flow: Reads cleanly: "When the whole water system's properly filled, the water'll start running out the overflow pipe onto the ground."
unharnessed.variety: Varied enough: "some such", "full stop", "dead sure", "hands down", "grunt", "had a bit of a go"; 'cause used three times.
unharnessed.essence: Clearly the manual's question-and-answer drill: "How do you use the Spark and Throttle Levers?"

yarn-dinkum.why: 'cos' carries nearly every causal clause; noticeable repetition.

yarn-troppo.why: An opener that hangs off nothing and sits oddly at the start of a pre-start checklist.

yarn-troppo.quote: if you can get it clean outta the tank
yarn-troppo.original: Soft rain water, when it is to be had in a clean state
yarn-troppo.why: Assumes a rainwater tank; a small invented detail.

dinkum-3.original: it is a good plan to examine the radiator frequently
dinkum-3.why: Beaut is a touch forced in a plain maintenance tip.

dinkum-3.quote: Usually ya want the spark lever
dinkum-3.original: The spark lever should usually be put in about the third or fourth notch
dinkum-3.why: The ya spelling is used nearly everywhere and becomes a tic.

engine.quote: After the engine has become flamin' limbered up
engine.original: After the engine has become thoroughly limbered up
engine.why: Flamin' replaces 'thoroughly', a wrong sense; it is an intensifier, not 'completely'.
US Gasoline left in the heading while the body says petrol; also carburetor and gas engine oil left.

engine.quote: Upon receipt of the car see that a supply of medium light, high-grade gas engine oil is poured
engine.original: Upon receipt of the car see that a supply of medium light, high-grade gas engine oil is poured
engine.why: Largely untranslated; far lighter than the level-5 brief.

unharnessed.quote: Leave the cock open till it stops running, then shut it.
unharnessed.original: Leave the cock open until it stops running—then close it.
unharnessed.why: Many lines are plain casual English; light for a level-5 brief.

summaries.yarn-dinkum: Faithful, natural and smooth; the Aussie fits the instructions exactly, a notch short of a full pub yarn.
summaries.yarn-troppo: The liveliest and most fully Aussie retelling, varied and faithful, with a couple of stray additions.
summaries.dinkum-3: Clean, faithful and natural, a little lighter than level 5 and without the mild swearing the brief allows.
summaries.engine: A rule-engine pass over the original: mostly untranslated, with a few bolted-on words, one of them in the wrong sense.
summaries.unharnessed: Natural, clear and faithful, with apt colour on the warnings, but lighter on Aussie than the brief asks.
